frameworks.name: Double-jeopardy sanity check on growth targets (penetration vs loyalty)
frameworks.decision: Whether a growth target should come mainly from more buyers or from more purchases per buyer, and whether a frequency-led target is realistic.
evidence_required: customers (or accounts) who bought in the last 12 months
purchases or visits per buyer in that period
rough count of category buyers in the reachable area (estimate allowed, labelled)
category purchase rate per buyer if known
prerequisites: a repeat-purchase category with several substitutes

branches.if: plan needs purchases per buyer to rise more than ~10-20% with flat buyer count
branches.then: flag as against double jeopardy; re-split the target toward penetration and show both versions

branches.if: required purchases per buyer exceed what buyers buy from the whole category
branches.then: mark infeasible (hard arithmetic, not a heuristic)

branches.if: category has few substitutes, high switching costs or a contract (SaaS seats, retainers)
branches.then: treat double jeopardy as context only; expansion revenue can be a real lever

branches.if: the business is capacity-limited
branches.then: do not set a penetration target above capacity; hand off to PB-capacity

steps: Decompose sales = buyers x purchases per buyer (code, not prose)
State the target in both terms
Check frequency against category rate and against peers if known
Prefer penetration levers (reach, availability, removing reasons not to buy) unless a branch above applies
exceptions_failure_modes: Contracted B2B or SaaS where 'frequency' is seat or usage expansion
One-off purchases (frequency always ~1)
Genuine niche with switching costs (Apple-type operating-system lock-in raised repeat only slightly)
Owner counts transactions not buyers

requirements.labor: owner exports buyer and order counts

metrics: share of new vs returning buyers
guardrails: Never present a frequency-only plan as the default for a repeat-purchase consumer business without the double-jeopardy note
stop_review: Review after one full purchase cycle; if buyers grew but frequency did not, that is the expected pattern, not failure
alternatives: No buyer-level data: use transactions and a customer-count estimate, labelled; or run a 4-week receipt or booking-name tally
No category size: skip penetration %, keep buyer counts
frameworks.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: double jeopardy is a strong default for consumer repeat-purchase businesses (cafés, salons, DTC consumables). For niche B2B, contracts and early-stage products it is a heuristic: the evidence base there is one concrete-supplier table and assertions in the FAQ.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed rule: when a plan's goal implies purchases-per-buyer growth above 20% with flat buyers in a repeat-purchase B2C business, the plan must also show the penetration-led version and label the frequency version as against the norm
proposed rule: required purchases per buyer greater than the category purchase rate is infeasible and must be blocked by a deterministic check
proposed rule: if buyer-level counts are missing, ask for them before setting a frequency target

frameworks.climbos_location: skills/growth-strategy/SKILL.md (goal decomposition); shared/growth/calc.ts (decomposition helper); skills/retention-lifecycle/SKILL.md (frequency plays framed honestly)

relation_to_existing.note: No existing guidance decomposes a sales goal into buyers x frequency or checks it against double jeopardy (grep found no mention in skills, playbooks or library books).

frameworks.disagreements: Retention-lifecycle and rebooking plays implicitly assume frequency is an easy lever. Sharp says it barely moves without penetration. Decided by the owner's own buyer x frequency history, and by the category (contracted B2B and SaaS expansion are outside his evidence).

frameworks.name: Retention vs acquisition allocation with a steady-state ceiling
frameworks.decision: How much effort goes to reducing churn/defection versus acquiring new customers, given the business's churn level, its size and whether churn is controllable.
evidence_required: churn reasons split: controllable (value, onboarding, service) vs uncontrollable (moved, closed, no longer needs, budget)
category or size-matched churn norm if any
prerequisites: consistent definition of an active customer

branches.if: churn is far above the reference range for the model and most of it is controllable (value, onboarding, failed payments)
branches.then: retention is the binding constraint (agrees with diagnosis.ts:131 and Verna EV-C2); acquisition continues at least at replacement level

branches.if: churn is within the normal range for a business of this size and most exits are uncontrollable
branches.then: treat acquisition as the growth lever; retention work is maintenance (Sharp ch3)

branches.if: business is small and its churn is higher than market leaders'
branches.then: expect some of the gap from size alone (retention double jeopardy); don't label it a product failure without churn reasons

branches.if: capacity is the limit
branches.then: neither; delivery constraint first (PB-capacity)

steps: Compute steady-state ceiling = new customers per month / monthly churn (code)
Compute replacement acquisition = churn x current base
Split churn reasons
Compare churn to a reference only where one exists (SaaS) and note size effect
Allocate: fix controllable churn first only when it is above the norm; never zero acquisition
exceptions_failure_modes: SaaS with high voluntary early churn: Sharp's low-defection examples do not apply
Very small bases: churn rates noisy month to month
Counting paused or seasonal customers as churned
metrics: share of churn that is controllable
guardrails: No '5x cheaper to retain' or '5% retention = 100% profit' claims (no empirical basis per ch3)
Retention plays must say what share of churn they can touch
stop_review: If a retention fix runs one renewal cycle and churn is unchanged, return effort to acquisition
alternatives: No churn reasons: run 5-10 exit interviews or a one-question cancel survey first
No churn rate: use repeat-rate proxy; mark retention 'unknown' (as diagnosis.ts:99 does for non-SaaS)
frameworks.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: Sharp's conclusion (acquisition dwarfs retention) depends on category-normal, low and largely uncontrollable defection. Small SaaS with 8-15% monthly churn sits outside that evidence; there, the steady-state ceiling makes retention decisive. Both views agree acquisition is never optional.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed rule: diagnosis output adds a computed steady-state ceiling (newCustomersPerMonth / monthlyChurn) and replacement acquisition (monthlyChurn x active customers) whenever both inputs exist
proposed rule: COMPETING.retention also names 'defection outside the business's control (moved, closed, no longer needs) and normal size-related churn'
proposed rule: block copy or plans that cite 'retention is 5x cheaper' or 'a 5% retention gain doubles profit' as fact
proposed rule: when retention binds, the plan still keeps acquisition at or above replacement level unless capacity binds
proposed rule: before labelling churn weak for a non-SaaS business, collect churn reasons

frameworks.climbos_location: shared/agents/diagnosis.ts (retention branch, COMPETING.retention, diagnosisBrief); skills/retention-lifecycle/SKILL.md; skills/growth-strategy/SKILL.md step 3

relation_to_existing.note: Candidate v2 of the retention branch: keeps the SaaS churn override but adds the ceiling, replacement-acquisition arithmetic and an uncontrollable-churn competing explanation.

frameworks.disagreements: Verna (02_activation_retention_plg.md) and growth-strategy SKILL.md:33 say fix retention before acquiring; diagnosisBrief (diagnosis.ts:149) says 'Don't add demand above it'. Sharp says acquisition drives growth and defection is mostly size and circumstance. What decides: churn level vs a size-matched norm, and the controllable share of churn reasons. High controllable churn: Verna wins. Normal churn: Sharp wins.

frameworks.name: Light buyers, real Pareto and buyer moderation (who to target)
frameworks.decision: Whether to concentrate marketing on current heavy/best customers or to reach light and non-buyers, and how to read 'top customers' analyses.
evidence_required: customer-level purchases for at least 12 months (ideally 24)
prerequisites: enough customers for deciles (rule of thumb: 100+)

branches.if: owner claims top 20% = 80% of sales without data
branches.then: ask for the export; default expectation for consumer repeat categories is about 50% (20:30:50), more extreme only over long periods

branches.if: plan targets only last year's heaviest buyers
branches.then: warn about buyer moderation and the heavy-buyer fallacy; add reach to light/non-buyers

branches.if: B2B with a few large contracts (revenue concentration by contract size, not purchase frequency)
branches.then: account concentration is a different quantity; key-account care is legitimate; don't apply 20:30:50

branches.if: capacity-limited service
branches.then: selecting higher-value clients is a capacity decision (PB-capacity), not a Pareto growth play

steps: Compute revenue share of top 20%, middle 30%, bottom 50% (code)
Compare two consecutive periods for the same customers before calling anyone 'VIP'
Size the light/non-buyer pool in reach
Allocate most acquisition effort to broad reach; keep heavy-buyer care cheap (service, not discounts)
exceptions_failure_modes: Short analysis windows exaggerate or understate concentration
One-off purchase categories
Account-based B2B
metrics: next-period share of last period's top 20%
share of sales from last period's non-buyers
guardrails: Don't build segments or lookalikes on a single period's heavy buyers without the moderation caveat
stop_review: If a heavy-buyer program shows member lift, check against the moderation baseline before expanding
alternatives: No customer IDs: skip; use category-buyer reach logic
frameworks.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: strong default for consumer repeat-purchase; for B2B prospecting from 'best customers' (skills/prospecting) the ICP is about fit, not purchase weight, so Sharp's fallacy applies only partly.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed rule: any 'top customers' statistic must come from data with the period stated; never assume 80/20
proposed rule: retention or VIP plays aimed at last period's heaviest buyers carry a note that next period they will buy less on average without any change (buyer moderation)
proposed rule: for B2C repeat-purchase businesses, at least one acquisition play reaches light or non-buyers of the brand

frameworks.climbos_location: skills/retention-lifecycle/SKILL.md; skills/plays-local/SKILL.md (#20 sms-vip-club); skills/prospecting/SKILL.md:13 (B2B: fit-based, keep)

relation_to_existing.note: No existing Pareto or buyer-moderation guidance; nothing in the repo asserts 80/20, so no contradiction to fix.

frameworks.disagreements: Prospecting and creator-scouting derive ICPs from 'best customers'. For B2B fit this is fine (Dunford). For consumer repeat-purchase, Sharp says the heaviest are already buying all they will. Decided by business type: fit-based B2B vs frequency-based B2C.

frameworks.name: Positioning mode: niche differentiation (Dunford) vs category-buyer distinctiveness (Sharp)
frameworks.decision: Whether positioning work should centre on a narrow best-fit segment and differentiated value, or on reaching all category buyers in reach with a distinctive, consistent brand identity.
evidence_required: number of viable substitutes buyers see as interchangeable
existing brand cues the business already uses consistently

branches.if: new or complex B2B/SaaS product, buyers compare features, few customers, early stage
branches.then: Dunford mode: best-fit segment, differentiated value, Big Fish default (BK03); add a light distinctiveness check

branches.if: consumer repeat-purchase or local everyday service with many interchangeable rivals (café, salon, bakery, DTC consumables)
branches.then: category-buyer mode: target all category buyers within physical reach; one or two relevant category cues; distinctive assets used consistently; differentiation claims optional

branches.if: a functional difference is real and large (allergy-free, premium tier, specialist)
branches.then: say it, but expect a partition, not a separate market; still reach the wider category

branches.if: segment narrowing is driven by geography or capacity
branches.then: compatible with Sharp: grow area by area with matched media (FAQ)

steps: Classify the category on the conditions above
Pick a mode and say why
In both modes run a brand-cue audit: which cues (name, colour, logo, character, tagline, style) the business uses and whether they are consistent across site, pack, posts and ads
If budget allows, test fame and uniqueness of 1-2 assets with category buyers
In category-buyer mode, the swap test is advisory, not a gate
exceptions_failure_modes: Using 'everyone' as an excuse to skip customer research
Sharp's evidence on low perceived differentiation is from mature consumer categories and retail banks; may not hold for new B2B tools
Rebrands on a whim destroy distinctive assets

requirements.measurement: fame = share linking asset to brand; uniqueness = share of those linking it only to this brand

guardrails: Never fabricate competitor gaps to create differentiation (existing BK03 rule)
Don't recommend a rebrand or new visual identity without evidence the current assets lack fame
stop_review: Revisit mode when evidence of a best-fit pattern appears, or when the business moves from niche to mass category
alternatives: No survey budget: audit consistency only and ask 5-10 customers what they recall
No brand cues yet: pick simple ones and keep them (social-visual-briefs provisional kit)
frameworks.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: Dunford answers 'what context makes our value obvious to buyers who evaluate'; Sharp answers 'how do near-substitutes win habitual choices'. Most ClimbOS SaaS and B2B owners fit Dunford; many local and DTC owners fit Sharp. Distinctiveness complements both.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed rule: positioning skill selects a mode (niche-differentiation or category-buyer) from category conditions and records why
proposed rule: in category-buyer mode, 'all category buyers in the service area' is an acceptable segment and the swap test is advisory
proposed rule: every positioning output includes a brand-cue consistency check across site, posts and ads
proposed rule: asset fame/uniqueness claims require survey data; otherwise label as unmeasured
proposed rule: which mode wins for early-stage local consumer brands is unknown; track outcomes by mode in bench

frameworks.climbos_location: skills/positioning/SKILL.md (steps 6-7, swap test line 57, segment rule line 70); skills/social-visual-briefs/SKILL.md; skills/meta-ads/SKILL.md

relation_to_existing.note: Contradicts the universal 'Big Fish default' and 'never everyone' for consumer repeat-purchase categories; extends with distinctive assets, which no current skill covers beyond a visual brand kit.

frameworks.disagreements: Dunford/BK03 make Big Fish, Small Pond the default and the positioning skill forbids 'everyone'. Sharp says competing brands sell to the same people, niches are mostly availability deficits, and perceived differentiation is low even for winners. What decides: purchase frequency, substitutability, whether buyers evaluate or choose by salience, and stage. Owner decision: Sharp is the default only for consumer repeat-purchase; heuristic elsewhere.

frameworks.name: Mental and physical availability: reach, continuity and branding in channel choice
frameworks.decision: How to weigh broad reach, continuous presence and ease of buying against high-intent demand capture when choosing and scheduling channels.
evidence_required: whether buyers search shortly before buying (recency category)
opening hours, ordering routes, delivery coverage

branches.if: recency category (emergency trades, legal, insurance, furniture, B2B with a trigger event)
branches.then: demand capture first (search, maps, directories), matches Sharp fn 69 and the current scoring intent weight

branches.if: recurring consumer category and budget can buy steady reach in the area
branches.then: add an always-on reach channel at even monthly spend; judge it over months, not weeks

branches.if: budget under ~$100-500/month
branches.then: reach media can't be bought at meaningful scale; use free reach (local listings, signage, partner newsletters, posts) and physical availability fixes

branches.if: physical availability is thin (hours, locations, delivery apps, checkout steps)
branches.then: fix availability before buying awareness; advertising falls flat if the brand is hard to buy

branches.if: new brand
branches.then: plant basics: what it is, what it looks like, where to buy; grow one area at a time with matched media

steps: Classify category recency and frequency
Audit physical availability (hours, locations, apps, stockists, booking friction)
Pick demand-capture channel(s) per scoring
If recurring B2C and budget allows, add one reach channel scheduled evenly
Brand-link every creative: brand cue in the first seconds or first frame and at the end
Judge reach channels on reach, branded recall proxies and slow sales trend
exceptions_failure_modes: Small budgets spread so thin that no one sees the ad more than once a quarter
Platform 'reach' that isn't attention (FAQ: social OTS vs actual brains)
Measuring brand reach by last-click ROAS and killing it in week 4

requirements.labor: owner time for listings and creative
requirements.measurement: reach and frequency from platforms; branded search; new-customer counts

guardrails: Even monthly spend preferred to bursts unless a seasonal peak is real
No paid reach without owner budget approval
Never treat impressions as people reached
stop_review: Reach channel: review at 3 months on new-buyer trend and branded search, not 8-week inquiries
alternatives: No ad budget: physical availability fixes, local listings, partner placements, consistent organic posting
No tracking: self-reported 'how did you hear' at checkout
frameworks.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: ClimbOS scoring already favours demand capture, which matches Sharp's own exception for recency categories and suits tiny budgets. The gap is recurring consumer businesses with real budgets, where the engine has no notion of reach, continuity or physical availability.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed rule: use the frequency dimension in scoring: for recurring B2C, soften the intent penalty on broad-reach families (paid_social, video, local, traditional) by a bounded amount when the budget band supports them
proposed rule: a physical-availability check (hours, ordering routes, stockists, booking friction) runs before any awareness spend for consumer businesses
proposed rule: paid reach plans spread spend evenly by month unless the owner names a seasonal peak
proposed rule: reach-channel stop rules use a 3-month window and new-buyer trend, not 8-week inquiries
proposed rule: whether reach channels beat demand capture for small recurring-B2C budgets is unknown; run a geo holdout when budget allows

frameworks.climbos_location: shared/acquisition/scoring.ts (priors, FACTORS, STAGE_INTENT); shared/acquisition/library.ts (Channel attributes); shared/playbooks/contracts.ts PB-social-content; skills/meta-ads/SKILL.md; skills/social-visual-briefs/SKILL.md

relation_to_existing.note: Book 05 separates demand creation and capture but gives no reach/continuity rule; Book 09 §3 says repetition builds memory but focuses on points of view, not brand cues. Reach and penetration do not enter channel scoring.

frameworks.disagreements: Sharp: reach light and non-buyers continuously; mass media is efficient. ClimbOS: intent-weighted scoring with tiny budgets and per-channel learning windows. Decided by recency vs habitual category, budget band, and frequency. meta-ads SKILL.md:114 ('never open with the brand name') vs Sharp's branding hurdle: reconcile by requiring a brand cue early (product in use, distinctive colour or name in frame) without a throat-clearing intro.

frameworks.name: Price promotion break-even and reach check
frameworks.decision: Whether to run a temporary discount, how deep, and what it can and cannot achieve.
evidence_required: expected volume lift (own history or a range)
share of promo buyers who bought before
prerequisites: owner confirms margin; ClimbOS never invents an offer

branches.if: expected lift < required lift = d/(m - d)
branches.then: the promotion loses contribution; recommend not running it or a shallower cut

branches.if: goal is new customers for an established brand
branches.then: say promo buyers are mostly existing buyers; prefer reach and availability

branches.if: new product trial or perishable capacity (empty slots, end of day)
branches.then: outside Sharp's evidence; a targeted, short offer can be rational (yield management)

branches.if: promotions are frequent (>1 in 4 weeks)
branches.then: warn about lowered reference price and promotion addiction; plan to wind down

branches.if: retailer requires promotions to keep listing
branches.then: evaluate against the listing objective, run the minimum needed

steps: Compute required lift (code)
Compare with expected lift; if unknown use elasticity -2.5 as a labelled central guess
Subtract a post-promo dip if stockpiling is possible
Prefer shallow cuts and feature/visibility support over depth
Report incremental contribution, not volume
exceptions_failure_modes: Ignoring baseline sales sold at a discount
Counting promo volume as new customers
Deep cuts eroding the reference price

requirements.capability: sales by day and by customer
requirements.measurement: baseline vs promo period; share of promo buyers who are new

metrics: share of promo buyers new to the brand
guardrails: No discount in a first lifecycle touch (agrees with skills/retention-lifecycle)
stop_review: Stop repeating a promo whose incremental contribution was negative
alternatives: No margin data: block the promotion recommendation until the owner gives it
No history: run one shallow, short test with a clear baseline window
frameworks.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: the break-even formula is exact; the elasticity values are dated FMCG averages and only a fallback. Perishable-capacity offers (salons, restaurants) are a different economic problem Sharp doesn't address.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed rule: add promoBreakEven(margin, discount) to shared/analysis/decisions.ts returning required lift = d/(m-d) and blocking promos where d >= m
proposed rule: a promotion play may not claim new-customer acquisition for an established brand without new-buyer data
proposed rule: no promotion recommendation without owner-confirmed margin
proposed rule: elasticity -2.5 is only a labelled fallback, never a forecast

frameworks.climbos_location: shared/analysis/decisions.ts (new calculator); skills/retention-lifecycle/SKILL.md (offer discipline); shared/playbooks/contracts.ts PB-pricing-test

relation_to_existing.note: Agrees with retention-lifecycle's discount discipline; adds the missing deterministic break-even and the reach/new-customer caveat.

frameworks.disagreements: Some local plays use offers to fill perishable capacity; that is consistent with Sharp only as capacity management, not brand growth. Decided by whether the unsold unit perishes.

frameworks.name: Loyalty programs, cross-sell and VIP clubs: what they can do and how to measure them
frameworks.decision: Whether to start a loyalty/points/VIP program or cross-sell push, what outcome to promise, and how to evaluate it without selection bias.
evidence_required: pre-period purchase history for members and non-members
who joins (existing heavy, existing light, new)
program cost incl. rewards given to people who would buy anyway
prerequisites: consented contacts for any messaging (existing rule)

branches.if: goal is growth (new buyers)
branches.then: a loyalty program is a weak lever: it recruits existing buyers; pair with reach

branches.if: goal is a consented contact list, data or a reason to message
branches.then: a low-cost card/club is reasonable; evaluate on list size and cost

branches.if: evaluation compares members vs non-members
branches.then: reject as biased; use pre/post with the same people, a holdout or the double-jeopardy benchmark

branches.if: cross-sell target of a big jump in products per customer
branches.then: flag as unlikely; differences between rivals are small

steps: State the program's real job
Cost rewards paid to buyers who would have bought anyway
Set an evaluation design before launch (holdout or pre/post on same customers)
Expect small effects
exceptions_failure_modes: Endowed-progress cards raise completion rates; completion isn't incremental sales
Coalition programs with competitor-store recruitment are rare
metrics: share of members who were new
guardrails: Never report member-vs-non-member gaps as program effect
stop_review: If incremental visits vs holdout are ~0 after 90 days, keep only if the list/data job justifies the cost
alternatives: No POS IDs: measure total visits vs prior-year same weeks, labelled weak
Small shop: a simple stamp card with no big promise
frameworks.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: the plays-local endowed-progress card is well supported for card completion but its 'visit frequency' tracking will overstate effects through selection and buyer moderation.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed rule: loyalty-program plays state their job (list, data, frequency nudge) and cannot be the only retention or growth play
proposed rule: evaluation of loyalty/VIP plays requires a holdout or same-customer pre/post; member vs non-member comparisons are rejected
proposed rule: diagnosis playStage treats 'loyalty program' as retention only when paired with a churn-reason fix

frameworks.climbos_location: skills/plays-local/SKILL.md #11 and #20; skills/retention-lifecycle/SKILL.md; shared/agents/diagnosis.ts:157 (playStage loyalty → retention)

relation_to_existing.note: plays-local rates the loyalty card 'evidence strong, predictability 4' on completion-rate evidence and tracks visit frequency of members; Sharp's evidence says the sales effect is small and the measurement biased.

frameworks.disagreements: plays-local (Nunes & Drèze field test) vs Sharp ch11. Both can be right: the card raises completion, which may barely change total visits. Decided by a holdout on total visits per customer.

frameworks.name: Applicability gate: when Ehrenberg-Bass laws are defaults vs heuristics for a small business
frameworks.decision: Which BK10 rules the engine applies as defaults, which as contextual heuristics, and which it sets aside, given category, purchase frequency, market size, capacity and stage.

branches.if: B2C, recurring/occasional, many substitutes, capacity not binding
branches.then: DEFAULT: K1, K3, K5 (reach/continuity), K6, K7 apply; positioning in category-buyer mode (K4)

branches.if: local service with emergency/recency buying (plumber, locksmith, lawyer)
branches.then: HEURISTIC: demand capture first; K5 reach only as cheap always-on; K2 acquisition emphasis holds

branches.if: niche B2B, few hundred reachable accounts, sales-led
branches.then: HEURISTIC: 'reach all category buyers' becomes 'cover the full reachable account list over time' rather than mass media; Dunford positioning default; K3 Pareto not applicable to contracts

branches.if: capacity-limited service (fully booked)
branches.then: SET ASIDE growth-by-penetration until capacity grows; PB-capacity and pricing first (diagnosis.ts:91-96,130)

branches.if: pre-launch or < ~20 customers
branches.then: HEURISTIC: no laws can be checked on own data; use only: plant basic memories, consistent cues, grow area by area; Dunford exploration mode

branches.if: subscription SaaS with churn above reference
branches.then: K2 retention branch overrides Sharp's acquisition emphasis

steps: Read profile dimensions
Assign each BK10 framework a status: default / heuristic / set aside
Pass statuses into the plan brief so agents cite them with the right strength
exceptions_failure_modes: Dimensions inferred with low confidence
Hybrid businesses (B2B2C, marketplaces) need per-side treatment
metrics: share of plans where status was set
guardrails: Never cite a BK10 law as certain for niche B2B, capacity-limited or pre-launch businesses (owner decision 2026-10-20)
alternatives: Unknown dimensions: ask the 1-3 dimension questions (scoring.ts dimensionsToConfirm) before applying any default
frameworks.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: Sharp claims universality (Preface 'Examples in this book'; FAQ 'What about small brands?'), but the evidence is overwhelmingly mature, repeat-purchase consumer categories with unconstrained supply. The gate turns the owner's decision into code-level statuses.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed rule: compute a BK10 applicability status per plan from customerType, frequency, salesMotion, capacity and customer count; agents must phrase BK10 claims at that strength
proposed rule: when capacity utilisation >= 0.8 (diagnosis.ts), penetration-growth advice is suppressed
proposed rule: in sales-led niche B2B, translate 'reach all buyers' into list coverage of the reachable account universe using only owner-sourced or public data (no assumed prospect database)
proposed rule: whether double jeopardy holds for small SaaS categories is unknown; collect owner data in bench before using it as a default

code_gaps.gap: The 'frequency' dimension (one_time/occasional/recurring) is declared but never read by priors() (scoring.ts:228-275), so purchase frequency cannot change channel ranking.
code_gaps.proposed_change: Use frequency with customerType: for recurring B2C, apply a bounded audience/intent adjustment to broad-reach families (paid_social, video_audio, local, traditional) when the budget band allows; leave one_time/recency categories unchanged.

code_gaps.gap: No reach or penetration factor: the 8 factors and STAGE_INTENT (unaware=30 vs high_intent=95, weight 0.2) structurally down-rank channels that build mental availability among light/non-buyers. Correct for tiny budgets and recency categories, but there is no condition where reach counts.
code_gaps.proposed_change: Candidate v2: optional 'reach' factor (share of category buyers in area reachable per month) with weight 0 by default and >0 only for recurring B2C at budget band >= $1,000-5,000; validate on bench before enabling.

code_gaps.gap: Channel has 'scale' (organic scalability) but no attribute for reach breadth or for always-on vs burst scheduling, so continuity advice can't be generated deterministically.
code_gaps.proposed_change: Add optional channel attributes reachBreadth (0-2) and schedule ('always_on'|'burst_ok'); scorecardText notes even monthly spend for reach channels.

code_gaps.gap: COMPETING.retention names only budget or seasonality; misses uncontrollable defection (moved, closed, no longer needs) and size-related churn (retention double jeopardy).
code_gaps.proposed_change: Extend the competing explanation text; when the owner gives churn reasons, show the controllable share.

code_gaps.gap: When retention binds, the brief says 'Don't add demand above it' with no arithmetic on the acquisition needed just to hold the base; Sharp (ch 3) shows acquisition is required even to maintain size.
code_gaps.proposed_change: Add deterministic readings: steadyStateCeiling = newCustomersPerMonth/monthlyChurn and replacementAcquisition = monthlyChurn x activeCustomers (needs an activeCustomers input); brief says keep acquisition at least at replacement.

code_gaps.gap: playStage maps any 'loyalty' wording to retention, so a points or stamp-card play satisfies lintDiagnosisFit for a retention constraint even though loyalty programs show small effects (ch 11).
code_gaps.proposed_change: Require a churn-reason fix (activation, payment recovery, service) alongside a loyalty play for the retention fit check, or warn when a loyalty program is the only retention play.

code_gaps.gap: No promotion break-even calculator; promo maths would be done in model prose.
code_gaps.proposed_change: Add promoBreakEven({margin, discount, expectedLift?}) returning requiredLift = d/(m-d), incremental contribution if expectedLift given, and error when d >= m; expose via calculate().

code_gaps.gap: PB-social-content stop rule 'No inquiries after 8 weeks' judges only demand capture; no consistency guardrail on brand cues.
code_gaps.proposed_change: Add guardrail 'same distinctive cues across posts' and note the stop rule measures inquiries only; brand-reach effects need a longer window.
